correctness.rationale: For every allowed base digraph and every attached ear, adjoining \(a_i\) to a face containing \(p_i\), or \(b_i\) to a face containing \(q_i\), extends a path at a fresh degree-one endpoint and cannot form a directed cycle or violate degree bounds. Hence \(\sigma\cup\rho(\sigma)\) is always a simplex, providing a simplicial retraction contiguous to identity and fixing the explicit join. Cone links at \(p_i\) and \(q_i\) give honest elementary collapse pairs in descending face dimension, independent across repeated roots. The integral suspension and character are standard join-chain facts; explicit signed orientation cycle determines the arm permutation sign and reversal parity. Standalone exhaustive tests of all faces in ten finite cases and group equivariance in stars with \(1\le m\le4\) independently corroborate, but do not replace, this all-order proof.

evidence: A source/sink directional suspension operation generally cannot be applied to a root that is an internal vertex of a directed cycle, while the new theorem can: the proof explicitly sends root-facing arcs to leaf-facing arcs.

The bidirected double-star theorem concerns edges incident directly to adjacent branching centres; the new once-subdivided star has an intermediate vertex on every arm and comes from the arbitrary-base ear collapse.

A disjoint-union join \(X(D\sqcup A_2)=X(D)*S^0\) is a known trivial suspension, but the new \(E_m\) is connected to the base at the roots, and the explicit collapse proves this attachment does not change the join type.

value.rationale: This is a local-to-global simple-homotopy and equivariant theorem for any finite digraph, not an arbitrary finite computation: it converts a connected, possibly cyclic bidirected attachment into the join with m zero-spheres, preserving all integral torsion through a known suspension shift and explicitly transferring automorphism representations. Source/sink restrictions in published multipath suspension constructions otherwise obstruct application at internal cyclic vertices. The natural family of all once-subdivided bidirected stars has a complete integral homotopy and symmetry classification. These consequences are useful structural reductions rather than only computational novelty.
